# HTTP 301 vs 308

## Short answer

Both 301 and 308 say that a resource has moved to a new permanent URI, and both are heuristically cacheable. They differ in what the client may do with the request method:

- **301:** for historical reasons, the client is allowed to turn a POST into a GET when it follows the redirect.
- **308:** the client keeps the same method, and in practice the same body.

Both are now defined in RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics).

## What each code means

**301 Moved Permanently.** The resource now has a new permanent URI, and future references should use it (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html, §15.4.2). The server SHOULD send a Location header with the preferred new URI, and the user agent MAY follow it automatically.

**308 Permanent Redirect.** RFC 9110 §15.4.9 uses almost the same wording: the resource has a new permanent URI that future references should use. It has the same SHOULD rule for the Location header (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html). RFC 7538, which created 308, describes it as the missing permanent counterpart of 307. It is similar to 301 "except that it does not allow changing the request method from POST to GET" (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7538.html).

## Request method and body

**General rule.** When a user agent follows a redirect automatically, it SHOULD resend the original request with a defined list of changes. One of those changes applies only "If the request method has been changed to GET or HEAD": the client then removes content-specific headers such as Content-Type and Content-Length (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html).

**301.** RFC 9110 says that, for historical reasons, a user agent MAY change the method from POST to GET for the follow-up request. If that is not wanted, the server should send 308 instead (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html). The RFC's history note explains the split:

- 307 and 308 were added to clearly mark redirects that keep the method.
- 301 and 302 were adjusted to allow POST to be redirected as GET.

MDN notes that the Fetch Standard, which governs browsers, does use GET after a 301 to a POST, "as permitted by the HTTP specification" (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/301). The Fetch Standard itself was not opened, so this point rests on MDN.

**308.** The method is preserved. RFC 7538 says 308 does not allow the POST-to-GET change (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7538.html). RFC 9110 classes 308 as "method-preserving" in its §15.4 note. Its §15.4.9 does not contain a "MUST NOT change the method" sentence; that wording appears in the 307 section.

**The request body.**

- MDN states that with 308 "the request method and the body will not be modified" (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/308).
- In the RFCs, the body consequence is an inference. Body-related headers are stripped only when the method becomes GET or HEAD. Under 308 the request is resent with the body. Under 301, a POST that becomes GET drops its body. Neither the RFC 9110 301 section nor the 308 section says this about the body in so many words.

**Sources disagree here.** MDN's 308 page says a 301 "requires the request method and the body to remain unchanged" and calls POST-to-GET "incorrectly handled by older clients" (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/308). That contradicts RFC 9110, which explicitly permits the change (MAY). It also contradicts MDN's own 301 page, which calls the change "permitted by the HTTP specification." RFC 9110 is the authoritative source.

## Caching

RFC 9110 §15.1 lists both 301 and 308 among the heuristically cacheable status codes (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html). Each code's own section repeats this. Such a response can be stored and reused unless the method definition or explicit cache controls say otherwise.

RFC 9111 (HTTP Caching) explains what "heuristically cacheable" means in practice (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111.html):

- If the server gives no explicit expiration time, a cache MAY estimate one, for example from Last-Modified. A typical fraction is about 10% of the time since that date.
- A cache MUST NOT use such an estimate when an explicit expiration time is present.

So an explicit `Cache-Control` directive overrides the default. MDN's example 301 response sends `cache-control: max-age=2592000,public`.

RFC 7538 described 308 as "cacheable by default" (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7538.html). This is not a conflict. RFC 9111 notes that older specifications used "cacheable by default" for what is now called "heuristically cacheable." RFC 9111 is the current caching specification and obsoletes RFC 7234.

## Where each code is specified

**Current specification.** Both codes are now defined in RFC 9110, *HTTP Semantics*: 301 in §15.4.2 and 308 in §15.4.9. RFC 9110's header lists the documents it obsoletes, including RFC 7231 and RFC 7538 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html).

**301 history.** The lineage runs RFC 2616 → RFC 7231 → RFC 9110. RFC 7231 (§6.4.2) obsoleted RFC 2616 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7231.html). RFC 9110 does not itself list RFC 2616 as something it obsoletes.

**308 history.**

- 308 was first published in the Experimental RFC 7238.
- RFC 7538, a Standards Track document, replaced RFC 7238 "with no technical changes" (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7538.html).
- RFC 9110 then obsoleted RFC 7538.
- RFC 7238 itself could not be opened (404). Its Experimental status is known only from RFC 7538's own wording.

**Deployment note.** RFC 9110 says 308 is "much younger (June 2014)" than its sibling codes and "might not be recognized everywhere." RFC 7538 notes that clients that do not know 308 treat it like 300 (Multiple Choices), so servers cannot rely on automatic redirection.
